description: I'm Yasin, a React and React Native developer (TypeScript, Firebase, Expo) with experience building business dashboards, mobile apps, and API integrations. For this hackathon I'm building a Martian Map: a tablet-style web app for an astronaut's Marswalk in the Gale Crater and Mount Sharp area. It layers real NASA data (orbital imagery, terrain, thermal), draws a walking route that avoids steep ground, and shows rover photos and safety notes for each science stop.
summary: Marswalk Navigator is a tablet-style mission console that helps an astronaut plan a Marswalk in the Gale Crater and Mount Sharp region, near the boxwork formations Curiosity studied in 2025. It layers real NASA data: Context Camera and HiRISE orbital photos, a 1 m USGS/NASA elevation model, MOLA relief shading, and THEMIS thermal imagery. From the elevation data we compute slope on a 10 m grid and plan a 2.9 km walk from a hypothetical habitat through four science stops, never crossing ground steeper than an assumed 20-degree limit. Explore mode plans a route to any tapped destination with safest, balanced, or fastest preferences and a return-to-habitat check. Each stop shows an orbital view of its exact spot, a real Curiosity photo of the area, local slope, and a safety rating, and a safety panel shows published Curiosity radiation measurements. Anything assumed or simplified is labeled in the app.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Marswalk Navigator is a hyperlocal map for one Mars surface excursion, built for the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge. The mission is the Boxwork Expedition near Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, the same kind of formation Curiosity studied in 2025. A 2.88 km route runs from a hypothetical habitat through four science stops. A briefing introduces the mission, then a map-first console shows layered NASA data, a walking route, stop cards, and a safety panel.

HOW IT WORKS

- Data layers: Context Camera photos (about 5 m per pixel), HiRISE close-up photos (about 64 cm per pixel when zoomed in), MOLA relief shading, and THEMIS thermal imagery, plus a slope layer computed from a 1 m USGS/NASA elevation model of Gale Crater.

- Routing: the elevation model is processed offline into a 10 m grid, where each cell keeps its steepest slope. An A* search plans the route. Cells steeper than an assumed 20-degree limit are blocked, and steeper cells cost more.

- Explore mode: tap any destination and a route is planned live in the browser, with Safest, Balanced, and Fastest preferences. A return check tests the round trip against an assumed 4-hour EVA window.

- Stops: each stop card shows an orbital HiRISE view of that exact spot, a real Curiosity photo of the boxwork area (labeled "not this exact spot", with its sol and credit), elevation, local slope, distance back to the habitat, and a safety badge.

- Safety: a route safety rating (1 to 3 stars) with its rule shown, slope statistics, and published Curiosity RAD radiation values for Gale Crater.

- Verification: "npm run verify" reproduces the headline numbers, including Bradbury Landing at -4501.09 m against the published -4501 m.

WHY IT MATTERS

Mars Trek and geologic maps cover regional and global views. An astronaut on one walk needs the ground, slope, safety information, and a plausible route in one place. Marswalk Navigator shows how existing NASA data can be layered for that job.

TOOLS

Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, deployed on Vercel. Heavy data processing runs offline in scripts, and the app loads small static files and computes routes in the browser.

HONEST LIMITS

- The habitat is hypothetical, and the stops were chosen from slope screening and the boxwork map.

- The 20-degree slope limit, the 3.5 km/h walking pace, and the 4-hour EVA window are assumptions, not NASA figures.

- Routing uses slope only. Individual rocks and soft ground are not modeled.

- There is no live current-conditions feed. Radiation values are published site-level measurements.

- The elevation model is a merged mosaic, so its detail varies across the area.

- Next steps: rock abundance, terrain softness, and USGS geologic maps as routing inputs, and a rover or astronaut pair splitting stops.

USE OF AI

AI tools were used to build this project. An AI coding agent helped write the application code, data-processing scripts, and documentation, and AI assistance helped draft the written text. I chose the challenge, location, data sources, safety rules, and assumptions, directed the work, and checked the results. No images or video were AI-generated. All map imagery and photos come from NASA missions and are credited.

SOURCE CODE

The source code is public on GitHub, and a full credits page is in the app at /credits.
